extracted.intended_audience: members of learned societies and educated readers interested in natural philosophy (18th-century scientific public)
extracted.subtask_description: A set of 18th-century essays and society-readings on natural philosophy topics (magnetism, seacoal, earthquakes, light/heat, and lightning protection) intended for correspondence and presentation to learned audiences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Equivalence of lightning and electric matter
rubrics_metrics.description: Experiments made in electricity first gave philosophers a suspicion that the matter of lightning was the same with the electric matter... Experiments afterward made on lightning obtained from the clouds by pointed rods... have since proved this suspicion to be perfectly well founded; and that, whatever properties we find in electricity, are also the properties of lightning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Empirical demonstration by drawing lightning from clouds with pointed rods, receiving it into bottles and subjecting it to trials; use experimental parity between small electrical experiments (sparks) and lightning to justify theoretical identification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nature of the electrical (lightning) fluid
rubrics_metrics.description: This matter of lightning or of electricity is an extreme subtile fluid, penetrating other bodies, and subsisting in them, equally diffused.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When one body has a greater proportion it will communicate to another until proportions equalize (if distance not too great or proper conductors exist). The fluid can pass through conductors (sometimes without light or sound) or through air (producing visible light and sound).

rubrics_metrics.name: Conductor vs non-conductor classification
rubrics_metrics.description: All metals and water are good conductors. Other bodies may become conductors by having some quantity of water in them... Glass, wax, silk, wool, hair, feathers, and even wood, perfectly dry, are non-conductors: that is, they resist instead of facilitating the passage of this subtile fluid.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize that moisture can turn otherwise poor conductors (e.g., wood) into conductors. Use this classification when assessing vulnerability of materials and structures to electrical discharge.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effect of conductor quality and size on damage
rubrics_metrics.description: If the conductor be good and of sufficient bigness, the fluid passes through it without hurting it. If otherwise, it is damaged or destroyed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design safety conductors large and continuous enough to carry discharge safely to ground; insufficient conductors may suffer damage and transfer dangerous currents to the surrounding structure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Striking distance concept
rubrics_metrics.description: The distance at which a body charged with this fluid will discharge itself suddenly... is different according to the quantity of the fluid, the dimensions and form of the bodies themselves, and the state of the air between them. This distance... is called the 'striking distance'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate potential for discharge by considering charge magnitude, geometry of objects, and atmospheric conditions; objects within striking distance may be subject to direct discharge unless effective conductors intervene.

rubrics_metrics.name: Protection by continuous metal roofs and downspouts
rubrics_metrics.description: Buildings that have their roofs covered with lead or other metal, the spouts of metal continued from the roof into the ground to carry off the water, are never hurt by lightning as, whenever it falls on such a building, it passes in the metals and not in the walls.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use metal roofing and continuous metal conductors to ground to protect buildings: ensure continuity from roof metal to earth so lightning current prefers metal path rather than structural materials.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tall trees and lofty buildings as imperfect conductors
rubrics_metrics.description: Tall trees and lofty buildings, as the towers and spires of churches, become sometimes conductors between the clouds and the earth; but, not being good ones, that is, not conveying the fluid freely, they are often damaged.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize vulnerability of tall structures that lack good, low-resistance conductors; adding proper conductors can reduce damage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pathways of discharge within structures and items attracting current
rubrics_metrics.description: When other buildings happen to be within the striking distance from such clouds, the fluid passes in the walls, whether of wood, brick, or stone, quitting the walls only when it can find better conductors near them, as metal rods, bolts, and hinges of windows or doors, gilding on wainscot or frames of pictures, the silvering on the backs of looking-glasses, the wires for bells, and the bodies of animals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify likely preferential conductors inside structures (metal fittings, wiring, metal ornamentation, animals) that can attract current and cause localized damage; mitigate by providing intentional, safe conductors to earth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of earthquake
rubrics_metrics.description: An earthquake is defined to be a vehement shake or agitation of some considerable place, or part of the earth, from natural causes, attended with a huge noise like thunder, and frequently with an eruption of water, or fire, or smoke, or winds, &c.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this broad definition when classifying seismic events and distinguishing them from lesser tremors or local ground disturbances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classification of earthquake motions
rubrics_metrics.description: Aristotle and Pliny distinguish two kinds, with respect to the manner of the shake, viz., a tremour and a pulsation; the first being horizontal, in alternate vibrations, compared to the shaking of a person in an ague; the second perpendicular, up and down... Agricola increases the number, and makes four kinds, which Albertus Magnus again reduces to three, viz., inclination (vibrates alternately right to left), pulsation (beats up and down), and trembling (shakes and totters every way).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Classify observed seismic motions into horizontal (tremour/inclination), vertical (pulsation), or multidirectional trembling to interpret damage patterns and eyewitness accounts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Earth's own structural collapse as cause of earthquakes
rubrics_metrics.description: The earth itself may sometimes be the cause of its own shaking; when the roots or basis of some large mass being dissolved, or worn away by a fluid underneath, it sinks into the same, and, with its weight, occasions a tremour of the adjacent parts, produces a noise, and frequently an inundation of water.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider subsidence into voids or weakened supports (dissolution, erosion) as a mechanism for localized seismic events and associated ground failures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Subterranean waters and heated fluids as causes
rubrics_metrics.description: The subterraneous waters may occasion earthquakes by their overflowing, cutting out new courses, &c. Add that the water, being heated and rarefied by the subterraneous fires, may emit fumes, blasts, &c., which, by their action either on the water or immediately on the earth itself, may occasion great succussions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Account for fluid movement, sudden release, or thermal expansion of underground waters as potential drivers of shocks and surface phenomena (e.g., hot springs, sudden ejections).

rubrics_metrics.name: Air (pent up vapours) as agent of earthquakes (Amontons' idea)
rubrics_metrics.description: The air may be the cause of earthquakes; for the air being a collection of fumes and vapours... if it be pent up in too narrow viscera of the earth, the subterraneous or its own native heat rarefying and expanding it, the force wherewith it endeavours to escape may shake the earth; hence there arises divers species of earthquakes, according to the different position, quantity, &c., of the imprisoned aura.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include the role of compressed, heated air or vapors in models of seismic activity and consider depth-dependent compression and thermal effects (Amontons' depth/pressure arguments).

rubrics_metrics.name: Fire/pyrites ignition hypothesis for earthquakes, thunder, lightning
rubrics_metrics.description: Fire is a principal cause of earthquakes; ... Dr. Lister is of opinion that the material cause of thunder, lightning, and earthquakes, is one and the same, viz., the inflammable breath of the pyrites, which is a substantial sulphur, and takes fire of itself. The same sulphurous smell being found in anything burned with lightning, and in the waters, &c., cast up in earthquakes... indicates this.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Correlate sulphurous odors, presence of pyrites, and explosive/combustive behavior underground with seismic and volcanic phenomena; regions rich in sulphur and nitre may be more earthquake-prone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dr. Woodward's subterranean-heat-and-water theory
rubrics_metrics.description: Subterraneous heat or fire (which is continually elevating water out of the abyss, to furnish the earth with rain, dew, springs, and rivers), being stopped in any part of the earth, and so diverted from its ordinary course by some accidental glut or obstruction... becomes preternaturally assembled in a greater quantity than usual into one place, and therefore causeth a great rarefaction and intumescence of the water of the abyss, putting it into great commotions and disorders... that this effort... splits and tears the earth, making cracks and chasms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use obstructions to subterranean flow and consequent build-up of heat/pressure as explanatory mechanism; view volcanoes as vents ('spiracles') that relieve such assemblies and reduce shaking where present.

rubrics_metrics.name: Volcanoes as vents (diverticula) decreasing earthquake violence
rubrics_metrics.description: Ætna, Vesuvius, Hecla, and the other volcanoes, are only so many spiracles, serving for the discharge of this subterraneous fire... That where there happens to be such a structure... as that the fire may pass freely, and without impediment, from the caverns wherein it assembles unto those spiracles, it then readily gets out, from time to time, without shaking or disturbing the earth; but where such communication is wanting... it heaves up and shocks the earth with greater or lesser impetuosity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpret active volcanic vents as pressure-relief features; absence of open conduits can increase subterranean pressure and earthquake severity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Chemical demonstration of artificial earthquakes
rubrics_metrics.description: To twenty pounds of iron filings add as many of sulphur; mix, work, and temper the whole together with a little water... This being buried three or four feet under ground, in six or seven hours time will have a prodigious effect; the earth will begin to tremble, crack, and smoke, and fire and flame burst through.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provides a laboratory/field demonstration linking sulphur/iron mixtures and ignition to ground disturbance; offered as an illustration of how subterranean chemical reactions could produce seismic-like effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Geological susceptibility indicators
rubrics_metrics.description: Those countries which are mountainous and cavernous, abounding with stone and marble, and affording sulphur and nitre in great plenty, are by far the most injured by earthquakes... England is so little troubled with earthquakes [because of] the paucity of pyrites in England.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess regional earthquake risk by noting mountainous/cavernous structures and presence of sulphurous minerals or nitre; historical comparisons (Italy vs England) support this criterion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Seacoal (coal) origin and emplacement
rubrics_metrics.description: The seacoal has a vegetable origin, and... has been formed near the surface of the earth; but, as preceding convulsions of nature had served to bring it very deep in many places, and covered it with many different strata, we are indebted to subsequent convulsions for having brought within our view the extremities of its veins.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use fossil plant impressions (e.g., leaves/fern figures in roof slate at Whitehaven) and mine observations of coal veins descending below sea-level as evidence for surface/near-surface vegetal origin and later burial by geological convulsions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Theory of light and heat as a subtile fluid
rubrics_metrics.description: Universal space... seems to be filled with a subtile fluid, whose motion or vibration is called light. This fluid may possibly be the same with that which... dilutes the substance by separating the constituent particles... it is then called natural heat; when too much, it is called fever; and when forced into the body in too great a quantity from without, it gives pain... and the fluid so entering and acting is called fire.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat light and heat as manifestations of a pervasive subtile fluid whose distribution and vibration account for illumination and thermal phenomena; apply concept to bodily heat (digestion) and combustion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conservation-like view of fire/heat
rubrics_metrics.description: If fire be an original element or kind of matter, its quantity is fixed and permanent in the universe. We cannot destroy any part of it, or make addition to it; we can only separate it from that which confines it, and so set it at liberty; as when we put wood in a situation to be burned...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpret combustion and heating as liberation and transfer of a preexisting fluid component (fire) from bodies; use this to reason about heat flow, burning, and thermal processes.
